42858907.label: Background
42858907.text: Quantitative assessment of myocardial blood flow (MBF) and myocardial flow reserve (MFR) is clinically superior to relative imaging but limited by dynamic scanning requirements. We evaluated a novel single-time-point (STP) method to estimate MBF from a single static image using a population-based power law model of the arterial input function.

42858907.label: Methods
42858907.text: The STP model was optimized using retrospective dynamic 13N-ammonia positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) data (N = 90) and prospectively validated in 31 symptomatic patients undergoing both dynamic 13N-ammonia PET (reference) and conventional 99mTc-MIBI single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT)/computed tomography (leave-one-patient-out cross-validation). STP estimates were compared against dynamic PET via correlation and Bland-Altman analyses.

42858907.label: Results
42858907.text: The STP model demonstrated stable performance across a wide postinjection window in PET. For 99mTc-MIBI SPECT, reproducibility coefficients for stress MBF (44%), rest MBF (58%), and MFR (67%) were comparable to PET test-retest literature. SPECT MBF 95% limits of agreement (range: 1.5 mL/g/min) approached or exceeded reported dynamic cadmium zinc telluride-SPECT benchmarks. Technical acquisition delays were the primary source of model degradation.

42858907.label: Conclusions
42858907.text: The simplified STP approach provides reliable MBF and MFR estimates from standard static scans, showing strong agreement with dynamic 13N-ammonia PET. By eliminating the requirement for full dynamic protocols, this method facilitates absolute flow quantification using existing conventional SPECT infrastructure.

42880957.text: PET is the most powerful imaging modality for studying neurotransmitters, receptors, and neuromodulation in humans, complementing the anatomic and hemodynamic information provided by MRI. However, PET temporal resolution remains constrained by sensitivity, limiting studies of fast, dynamic neurochemical processes. To address this gap, we are developing the Human Dynamic NeuroChemical Connectome, an imaging system integrating NeuroSphere PET, a novel ultra-high-sensitivity dedicated brain PET camera, with the Siemens Healthineers Magnetom Terra.X, a clinical 7-T MRI scanner. This article describes the design, engineering, and simulation-based performance estimation of NeuroSphere PET. Sensitivity maximization drove 2 core design choices: a partial spheric detector arrangement with a 32-cm inner diameter and 70% solid-angle coverage and the use of 26-mm lutetium oxyorthosilicate crystals for high stopping power (∼90% at 511 keV), coupled to silicon photomultipliers in a light-sharing, depth-of-interaction-capable configuration. The system comprises 872 detector blocks organized across 19 rings and 218 modules. At the detector level, measured performance includes energy resolution of approximately 11% full width at half maximum (FWHM), depth-of-interaction resolution of approximately 8 mm FWHM, and coincidence timing resolution of approximately 500 ps FWHM. System-level performance was evaluated using the ultrafast Monte Carlo PET simulator, accounting for realistic detector response, positron range, photon noncollinearity, and interdetector scatter. Sensitivity was estimated from a 30-cm uniform sphere, predicting a peak sensitivity of about 38% and a whole-brain average exceeding 25%. Spatial resolution and image quality were assessed through Derenzo phantom simulations evaluated at both the center of the field of view and 8 cm off-center, indicating that 1.6-mm structures can be resolved near the center of the field of view and that resolution of less than 2 mm can be maintained at the cortex. The system incorporates a 3-dimensional-printed MRI-compatible gantry, a dedicated 16-channel parallel transmit-receive radiofrequency head coil, and a custom radiofrequency shielding enclosure for simultaneous PET/MRI at 7 T. By targeting sensitivity an order of magnitude higher than that of commercial PET systems, NeuroSphere PET is expected to enable simultaneous neurochemical and hemodynamic studies with substantially improved spatiotemporal resolution, providing new insights into brain function and connectivity.

42925457.label: Background
42925457.text: Patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) exhibit an elevated risk of cardiovascular events, with imaging-based risk stratification becoming increasingly important. This study compares the prognostic utility of [13N]NH3 PET/CT assessing myocardial blood flow (MBF), coronary flow reserve (CFR) and coronary artery calcium score (CACS) as well as 3D carotid ultrasound (for carotid plaque burden; cPB) in hemodialysis (HD) versus peritoneal dialysis (PD) patients listed for kidney transplantation.

42925457.label: Results
42925457.text: 41 ESRD patients (HD n = 31; PD n = 10; median follow-up 4.9 years) without known coronary artery disease underwent myocardial perfusion imaging with [13N]NH3 PET/CT, CACS, and 3D carotid ultrasound. HD patients exhibited lower myocardial stress blood flow (MBFstress) and CFR compared to PD patients (2.67 ± 0.67 vs. 2.97 ± 0.69; p = 0.24 and 2.5 ± 0.74 vs. 3.08 ± 1.12; p = 0.07). In the HD subgroup, only MBFstress correlated inversely with CACS and cPB (r = -0.32; p < 0.05 and r = -0.44; p < 0.05), whereas CFR did not (r=-0.14; p = 0.47 and r= -0.14; p = 0.44). On the other hand, both MBFstress and CFR were predictive of cardiovascular events in HD patients, although the number of events was low (n = 4). In contrast, PD patients exhibited only one single cardiovascular event in the follow-up and no significant imaging correlations were observed.

42925457.label: Conclusions
42925457.text: MBFstress and CFR may emerge as prognostic markers for cardiovascular events in HD patients whereas their prognostic power in PD patients remains uncertain. HD patients show more pronounced impairment in MBFstress and atherosclerotic plaque burden in the carotid artery, highlighting particularly this parameter as a prognostic marker in this group.

42949357.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) creates new susceptibility to diagnostic error in radiology related to the cognitive processes by which radiologists' interpretations incorporate AI outputs. This Perspective presents a conceptual framework for cognitive biases in AI-assisted radiology linking specific biases to radiologist-AI interactions. The framework uses dual-process theory, recognizing fast intuitive and deliberate analytic modes of information processing, as an organizing model for understanding cognitive processes underlying radiologists' decisions and their potential contribution to bias. Across seven decision scenarios spanning image viewing, findings interpretation, and contextual integration, the framework examines how AI output timing, radiologist-AI agreement, trust calibration, and reader expertise influence decision-making. We identify adaptive heuristics that support efficient decisions but, when misapplied or overrelied upon, increase susceptibility to complacency, confirmation, automation, distrust, anchoring, and usual implication bias, and increase behavioral risk of use without qualification. We highlight AI paradoxes emerging from the framework of despecialization, system fragility, and deskilling. Finally, we propose strategies targeting these cognitive biases, including education and experiential learning, workflow and interface design, clinical oversight, and performance monitoring. This framework provides a structured basis for generating testable hypotheses and designing AI-assisted radiology systems that preserve the strengths of human expertise and AI while supporting calibrated reliance.

42975307.text: Background Multiple myeloma (MM) imaging is currently suboptimal, which may limit patient care. Zirconium 89 (89Zr) deferoxamine (DFO)-daratumumab is a novel CD38-targeted immuno-PET tracer. Purpose To compare 89Zr-DFO-daratumumab PET/CT against standard-of-care fluorine 18 (18F) fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT for detection of MM. Materials and Methods Participants with MM were accrued to this prospective phase 2 trial between March 2022 and July 2025. Standard-of-care 18F-FDG PET/CT and bone marrow biopsy were performed, along with research 89Zr-DFO-daratumumab PET/CT. If there were discrepant lesions between the two scans, image-guided biopsy was considered as the reference standard. The McNemar test was used to compare disease detection between the two imaging modalities. Results This study included 60 participants (median age, 63 years [IQR, 57-71 years]; 32 women). 89Zr-DFO-daratumumab PET/CT demonstrated at least one positive lesion in 43% (26 of 60; 95% CI: 31, 57) of participants, and 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated at least one positive lesion in 47% (28 of 60; 95% CI: 33, 60) of participants. While there was no overall difference in disease detection between the two imaging modalities (P = .81), MM was demonstrated only with 89Zr-DFO-daratumumab PET/CT in 13% (eight of 60) of participants, with subsequent biopsy confirmation of active myeloma. Conclusion In participants with MM, CD38-targeted 89Zr-DFO-daratumumab immuno-PET helped detect active myeloma in some participants with no signs of disease at 18F-FDG PET/CT.

42975707.label: Objectives
42975707.text: The efficacy of transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) plus targeted therapy and immunotherapy in unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is limited by variable responses. We aimed to develop and validate an integrated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-pathology model for response prediction and survival stratification (IMPRESS), which combines pretreatment MRI habitat radiomics and paired biopsy whole-slide images (WSIs) pathomics.

42975707.label: Materials and methods
42975707.text: This multicenter, retrospective study enrolled patients with unresectable HCC receiving TACE plus targeted therapy and immunotherapy from January 2019 to December 2024. Eligibility required pretreatment MRI and paired biopsy WSIs within 1 month before therapy, Child-Pugh class A/B, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status ≤ 1, and at least one measurable intrahepatic lesion ≥ 1 cm. Patients with missing or poor-quality MRI or WSIs, prior locoregional or systemic HCC therapy, second malignancy, ECOG ≥ 2, or incomplete data were excluded. Habitat MRI radiomics, WSI pathomics, and clinical features were integrated into IMPRESS. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Single-cell analysis was performed to explore the biological basis of the IMPRESS predictions.

42975707.label: Results
42975707.text: Among 231 patients, 94 (40.7%) achieved a treatment response. IMPRESS achieved AUCs of 0.957 (95% CI: 0.931-1.0), 0.878 (95% CI: 0.789-0.966), and 0.875 (95% CI: 0.782-0.966) in the training, validation, and test cohorts, respectively. Predicted responders and non-responders showed significantly different overall survival in all cohorts (all p < 0.001). Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed distinct immune and proliferative patterns consistent with model predictions.

42975707.label: Conclusion
42975707.text: IMPRESS model may provide a promising tool for pretreatment response prediction and survival risk stratification in unresectable HCC undergoing TACE-based combination therapy.

42975707.label: Key points
42975707.text: Question Reliable pretreatment tools are needed to identify unresectable HCC patients likely to benefit from TACE plus targeted therapy and immunotherapy. Findings An integrated MRI-pathology model combining habitat radiomics and deep-learning pathomics predicted treatment response, with validation and testing areas under the curve of 0.878 and 0.875. Clinical relevance The integrated model may support pretreatment response stratification for TACE-based triple therapy and help inform surveillance intensity or alternative treatment considerations, pending prospective validation.

42982907.label: Objectives
42982907.text: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of CT-derived fractional flow reserve (CT-FFR) for detecting haemodynamically significant coronary disease in patients with anatomically long-segment lesions.

42982907.label: Materials and methods
42982907.text: This retrospective multicentre study included patients who underwent coronary CT angiography and invasive pressure-wire FFR within 30 days. Anatomically long-segment disease was defined as lesion length ≥ 20 mm. Invasive FFR ≤ 0.80 was the reference standard. CT-FFR was assessed at vessel and patient levels, with patient-level CT-FFR defined as the minimum value per patient and patient-level disease as any invasive FFR ≤ 0.80. Diagnostic discrimination, threshold-based classification, and Bland-Altman agreement were evaluated.

42982907.label: Results
42982907.text: The diagnostic cohort included 329 patients and 377 vessels; 137 patients and 144 vessels had anatomically long-segment disease. At the vessel level, CT-FFR achieved an AUC of 0.941 (95% CI: 0.917-0.966), sensitivity of 94.3%, specificity of 83.7%, and accuracy of 88.6%. In anatomically long-segment vessels, the AUC was 0.961 (95% CI: 0.922-1.000), with sensitivity of 95.7%, specificity of 92.2%, and accuracy of 94.4%. At the patient level, the overall AUC was 0.941 (95% CI: 0.915-0.967) and 0.971 (95% CI: 0.934-1.000) in anatomically long-segment disease. Mean bias was small, although limits of agreement were clinically relevant.

42982907.label: Conclusion
42982907.text: CT-FFR showed high diagnostic discrimination for invasive FFR-defined ischaemia, including in anatomically long-segment disease. However, agreement limits and threshold-zone uncertainty support its use as a non-invasive physiological adjunct rather than a direct substitute for invasive pressure-wire assessment.

42982907.label: Key points
42982907.text: Question Does machine learning-based CT-FFR maintain diagnostic performance for invasive FFR-defined ischaemia in anatomically long-segment coronary lesions? Findings CT-derived FFR showed high diagnostic discrimination overall and maintained performance in anatomically long-segment disease, although subgroup comparisons remained exploratory. Clinical relevance CT-derived FFR may provide non-invasive physiological information in anatomically long-segment coronary disease before invasive angiography, while values near the 0.80 threshold require cautious interpretation.

43015507.label: Background
43015507.text: The signal regulatory protein alpha (SIRPα) receptor on myeloid cells binds cluster of differentiation (CD) antigen CD47 on tumor cells, resulting in a "don't eat me" signal that inhibits phagocytosis. BI 765063, an anti-SIRPα antibody, may restore anti-tumor immunity by blocking this interaction. This phase I study aimed to assess target engagement and blockade of BI 765063 using quantitative 89Zr-immuno-PET, incorporating a previously developed correction method for non-target-mediated antibody catabolism. For this, four patients with advanced cancer received two cycles of [89Zr]Zr-BI 765063 and underwent three PET-scans per cycle up to 120 h post injection. The first cycle included a low dose of BI 765063 and the second a dose more than 20 times higher, intended to block the target. Directly after BI 765063 administration at the second cycle, ezabenlimab was administered to start the investigational treatment of the patients (BI 765063 + ezabenlimab, both every 3 weeks). Tumor uptake was corrected for antibody catabolism using literature-based reference values and normalized to plasma activity to calculate corrected tissue-to-plasma ratios (cTPR). Patlak analysis with the cTPR values yielded corrected net irreversible uptake rates (cKi). PET data were compared with RNA-sequencing data and macrophage marker immunohistochemistry.

43015507.label: Results
43015507.text: All ten tumor lesions showed target engagement by cTPR values at 120 h exceeding reference values. Positive cKi values were observed in all but one lesion, in which no Patlak analysis could be performed. cTPR values were lower for the blocking dose than the low dose, with five out of ten lesions within the range of non-target-mediated uptake, indicating partial target blockade. Target engagement observed by PET was supported by positive SIRPα mRNA expression and myeloid cell presence.

43015507.label: Conclusion
43015507.text: Target engagement and blockade of BI 765063 were observed across all tumors, highlighting the potential of non-target-mediated antibody catabolism correction through cTPRs to improve quantification of target specific uptake with immuno-PET.

43064857.label: Background
43064857.text: Noninvasive staging of liver fibrosis is essential in chronic liver disease (CLD). Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) is well validated but requires dedicated hardware, whereas the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) derived from conventional diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) lacks specificity. Restriction spectrum imaging (RSI) decomposes the diffusion signal into multiple compartments and may capture fibrosis-related microstructural changes.

43064857.label: Purpose
43064857.text: To investigate the feasibility of RSI for noninvasive liver fibrosis staging in CLD and to compare its diagnostic performance with that of MRE, using liver biopsy as the reference standard.

43064857.label: Methods
43064857.text: This retrospective study included 100 consecutive patients with CLD who underwent liver biopsy, 3.0-T multi-b-value DWI (nine b values, 0-1500 s/mm²), and MRE within 6 months. Multi-compartment RSI models (K = 2-5) were fitted to region-of-interest-averaged signals, and the optimal model was selected using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). An RSI liver fibrosis index (RSI-LF) was derived from compartment fractions using ordinal logistic regression and internally validated with 1000 bootstrap resamples. AUCs of RSI-LF were compared with those of MRE and ADC using the paired DeLong test.

43064857.label: Results
43064857.text: The five-compartment RSI model (RSI5) showed the lowest BIC. The second and fourth fractions, K5C2 and K5C4, correlated positively (ρ = 0.53) and negatively (ρ = -0.55) with fibrosis stage (both false discovery rate [FDR]-adjusted p < 0.001). RSI-LF yielded AUCs of 0.774 (95% CI: 0.651-0.898), 0.863 (0.793-0.933), and 0.911 (0.842-0.981) for ≥F2, ≥F3, and F4, respectively, with negligible bootstrap optimism. AUCs did not differ significantly from those of MRE at any threshold (all p > 0.05). RSI-LF also outperformed ADC at the ≥F3 and F4 thresholds (both p < 0.001).

43064857.label: Conclusion
43064857.text: Five-compartment RSI provides diffusion metrics associated with histologic fibrosis stage, and RSI-LF showed diagnostic performance numerically comparable to that of MRE. RSI is a promising microstructure-sensitive biomarker for liver fibrosis staging that warrants multicenter validation.

43077107.label: Purpose
43077107.text: To compare [68​Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 and [18F]FDG PET/CT for initial staging of breast cancer and assess the incremental clinical impact of FAPI findings.

43077107.label: Methods
43077107.text: This retrospective single-centre study included 83 patients with newly diagnosed invasive breast cancer who underwent both examinations within 7 days before treatment. Patient- and lesion-level detection, paired SUVₘₐₓ, histology-specific FDG non-detection, stage migration, additional biopsy, treatment modification, and progression-free survival (PFS) were evaluated using a composite reference standard. Generalised estimating equations accounted for within-patient lesion clustering.

43077107.label: Results
43077107.text: Patient-level positivity was 98.8% (82/83) for FAPI and 91.6% (76/83) for FDG (two-sided exact McNemar p = 0.031). FAPI detected 98.7% (235/238) of reference-positive lesions versus 67.2% (160/238) with FDG (p < 0.001); 76 lesions were FAPI-positive/FDG-negative and one was FDG-positive/FAPI-negative. Among 159 matched lesions, median SUVₘₐₓ was 12.10 for FAPI and 3.90 for FDG (p < 0.001). FDG non-detection was more frequent in invasive lobular carcinoma than in invasive ductal carcinoma/no special type (49.0% vs 30.1%; clustered odds ratio, 2.13; 95% CI, 1.004-4.54; p = 0.049). FAPI findings resulted in stage migration in 19.3%, additional biopsy in 18.1%, and treatment modification in 21.7% of patients. FAPI-only disease was not significantly associated with PFS (p = 0.343).

43077107.label: Conclusion
43077107.text: [68​Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT detected substantially more breast, nodal, and osseous lesions than [18F]FDG PET/CT and provided verified findings that altered staging and management. FAPI PET/CT may serve as a complementary initial-staging modality, particularly when FDG avidity is low; prospective multicentre validation is required.

43080107.label: Background
43080107.text: Prior hip surgery is common in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and it may complicate large-bore femoral access through surgical manipulation or scarring.

43080107.label: Aims
43080107.text: This analysis aims to evaluate whether previous hip surgery affects iliofemoral anatomical complexity or increases vascular access complications during transfemoral TAVR.

43080107.label: Methods
43080107.text: This single-center analysis from the BernTAVI Registry included 1791 consecutive patients undergoing transfemoral TAVR between 2014 and 2022. Patients were classified according to prior hip surgery concordant with the main access side for TAVR versus no or discordant hip surgery. Primary endpoints were vascular access complications and any bleeding at 30-day follow-up.

43080107.label: Results
43080107.text: Prior hip surgery was present in 354 patients (19.8%), including 235 with surgery concordant with the main access side. The remaining 1556 patients had no prior or discordant hip surgery. Computed tomography (CT) lumen-based iliofemoral complexity was comparable between groups (median Hostile score 1 in both; p = 0.725). Concordant hip surgery was not statistically significantly associated with vascular access complications (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 1.10, 95% CI 0.77-1.57; p = 0.610) or any bleeding (adjusted OR 1.25, 95% CI 0.89-1.75; p = 0.197) at 30 days. Major vascular access complications, major bleeding, 30-day and 1-year mortality, and cerebrovascular event risks were similar between groups. An exploratory subgroup of revision hip surgery (n = 23) showed higher bleeding risk. The CT-derived Hostile score was the strongest predictor of vascular access complications.

43080107.label: Conclusions
43080107.text: Among patients selected for transfemoral TAVR, prior concordant hip surgery was not statistically significantly associated with CT lumen-based iliofemoral complexity, vascular access complications, or bleeding. As operator-level access and closure techniques, femoral artery depth, and hip surgical approach were not captured, these findings warrant confirmation in prospective studies.

43086457.label: Purpose
43086457.text: Fibroblast activation protein (FAP)‑positive cancer‑associated fibroblasts contribute to immune exclusion and resistance to checkpoint blockade in the tumor microenvironment (TME). This study evaluated whether 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr, a FAP‑targeted alpha‑emitting radiopharmaceutical, could remodel the TME and enhance responsiveness to PD-L1 blockade.

43086457.label: Methods
43086457.text: Given the complex and immune-excluded microenvironment of lung cancer, we analyzed public datasets to define the clinical and immune context of FAP in this malignancy. 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr was synthesized and characterized for radiochemical purity, stability, FAP‑specific uptake, DNA damage, and PD‑L1 induction. Biodistribution, PET/CT imaging, therapeutic efficacy, histology, immune remodeling, and systemic cytokine profiles (MSD platform) were assessed in LLC/3T3‑FAP tumor‑bearing mice treated with saline, 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr, TPP-1 (a PD-L1-blocking peptide), or combination.

43086457.label: Results
43086457.text: FAP was enriched in stromal regions and correlated with advanced stage, reduced CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, and immunosuppressive signatures. 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr showed > 95% radiochemical purity, FAP‑dependent uptake, induced γ‑H2AX foci, and upregulated PD‑L1 in vitro. Tumor uptake peaked at 5.63 ± 0.72%ID/g (1 h) and remained 4.53 ± 2.13%ID/g at 24 h. Combination therapy exhibited the most potent tumor growth inhibition, reduced 18F‑FDG uptake, increased PD-L1-specific 68​Ga-TPP-1 uptake, decreased proliferation and angiogenesis, and enhanced CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration and granzyme B expression. At the immunological level, MSD‑based cytokine analysis revealed that combination therapy induced more extensive alterations in systemic immune modulation than either monotherapy, whereas 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr alone shifted the profile toward pro‑inflammation. No overt organ histopathology or sustained body-weight loss was observed during the assessment period (8 days), while treatment-associated haematological changes (reduced WBC and RBC counts) were detected.

43086457.label: Conclusion
43086457.text: In the engineered LLC/3T3-FAP model, 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr selectively targets FAP-rich tumor stroma, induces DNA damage and adaptive PD-L1 upregulation, and is associated with a shift of the immune-excluded TME toward a state that is more responsive to PD-L1 blockade. These findings suggest that FAP-targeted alpha radiotherapy may be a promising strategy for TME remodeling and immunotherapy sensitization in preclinical NSCLC models, and support further investigation toward clinical translation in more physiologically relevant systems.
